shippingNews.postTitle: Harriet M Joins Thunder Bay Tug Services Fleet

stories.body: A new tugboat has joined Thunder Bay Tug Services Ltd. with the arrival of Harriet M in Thunder Bay on October 8, 2026. The tug was acquired from Moran Towing Corporation of Philadelphia, PA. Built in 1978 at Jakobson Shipyard in Oyster Bay, NY, Harriet M measures approximately 28 metres in length and is powered by 3,005 horsepower. She will assist commercial vessels navigating the harbor and support ship movements throughout the Port of Thunder Bay as part of Thunder Bay Tug Services Ltd.’s operations, Michael Hull Harriet M arriving at the Port of Thunder Bay. todayInHistory.title: Sam Laud
todayInHistory.text: Sam Laud Bay Shipbuilding Corp. of Sturgeon Bay, WI, laid the keel for their hull # 712 on Jan. 4, 1974 to be built as a smaller-sized Great Lakes self-unloading bulk cargo carrier. The new vessel was launched on Nov. 19, 1974 for Buffalo's American Steamship Co. (ASC), a subsidiary of GATX Corp., Chicago, IL. Completed in 1975, the self-unloader was christened Sam Laud by Mrs. Edna Laud on behalf of her husband at a christening ceremony held April 15, 1975. Mr. Laud was the former president (1945) and chairman of the board (1956) of GATX Corp., having started with the company in 1916 as shop painter and riveter. Mr. Laud died August 1, 1963. GATX Corp. had acquired ASC in July of 1973. Mrs. Laud was accompanied by Mr. Frederick G. Jaicks, chairman and CEO of Inland Steel Co., Chicago, IL, who gave the address at the christening ceremonies. One of a new generation of self-unloaders for the ASC fleet, the Sam Laud was built at an approximate cost of $13.3 million and was the fourth of 10 self-unloaders launched for the fleet under Chapter XI of the Merchant Marine Act of 1970. Under this act, the U.S. government-guaranteed financing and tax deferred benefits for fleet modernizing. The other ASC self-unloaders built under this program were the Roger M. Kyes (now Adam E. Cornelius, 1973), Charles E. Wilson (now John J. Boland, 1973), H. Lee White (1974), St. Clair (1976), Belle River (now Walter J. marineWeather.synopsis: Lake Superior is currently between a 30.5 inch high offshore of New England and a 29.6 inch low stretched out from Nebraska toward James Bay. Throughout today, the low splits and weakens into a pair of 29.7 inch lows, one that remains in the Central Plains and another that moves eastward into Quebec. This will drag a 29.8 inch low across Lake Superior tonight into Monday morning as 30.3 inch high pressure expands across the Ontario and Manitoba shores of Hudson Bay. By Monday night, the high will weaken to 30.2 inches over Quebec as the Plains low moves into the Upper Great Lakes region at 29.7 inches. As the low escapes to New England Tuesday into Wednesday morning, a new 30.2 inch high forms over the Dakotas, moving over Lake Superior at 30.3 inches Wednesday night. Thursday, the high shifts toward New England as a 29.8 inch Alberta Clipper swings southeast through Manitoba. The Alberta Clipper tracks over Lake Superior Friday morning, followed closely by massive high pressure reaching from Nunavut to Texas.

marineWeather.synopsis: Light to modest south winds continue through Monday as broad low pressure lingers over the Upper Mississippi River Valley. This low pressure, around 29.6 inches, will tighten up and track northeastward across central Lake Michigan late Monday into early Tuesday, with chances for isolated thunderstorms. Northwest winds arrive behind the associated cold front into Tuesday, veering northerly or even northeasterly into Wednesday. A stronger low pressure system is possible later this week, which could bring gusty east to southeast winds and shower / storm chances into Thursday. The associated cold front and incoming strong high pressure may then yield gusty northwest winds Friday into Saturday, with gales possible.

Remnants from Hurricane Isaias, 29.80 inches, will move from the Ohio River Valley into New England today. Low pressure, 29.60 inches, will then push from the central Plains into the Great Lakes Tuesday morning, bringing the next potential for rain showers and isolated thunderstorms.

The remnant low of Isaias 29.90 inches will continue northeast through the central Appalachians today then offshore of the Mid Atlantic by Monday. A cold front with pressure of 29.70 inches will settle south across Lake Erie by Tuesday night. This front will remain just south of Lake Erie through Wednesday before finally pushing into the Ohio Valley Wednesday night and Thursday as high pressure 30.30 inches builds into the Upper Great Lakes.

A high pressure ridge averaging 30.1 inches continues to slowly exit eastward and briefly replaced by a weak trough averaging 29.8 inches. Behind the trough, a weak ridge averaging 29.9 inches slides eastward across the lake on Monday, exits eastward Monday night, and is followed by a cold front sweeping southeastward across the lake on Tuesday. Behind the cold front, a ridge averaging 30.2 inches builds from northern Ontario through Thursday.
